newsitem.title: FRANCE: Slumping Eurotunnel shares "for speculators only".
newsitem.headline: Slumping Eurotunnel shares "for speculators only".

text.p: Just when it appeared to have yanked its head above water, investors pummelled Eurotunnel on Wednesday by selling the Channel Tunnel operator's shares down in London and Paris for the second day running.
As details of a hard-fought debt relief agreement with Eurotunnel's banks sank in, the verdict from the stock markets was: "Leave it to the speculators".
Prospects for profits and dividends were just too intangible and too far off to put a value on the shares with any degree of certainty, analysts and traders in Britain and France said.
"Basically the share's worth nothing any longer. Speculators buy and sell and play with it, it keeps the market occupied," said one analyst at a Paris stockbroker.

Eurotunnel's stock tumbled to 6.95 francs in morning business in Paris with 10 million shares changing hands before trading calmed and the stock clawed back to 7.50 francs, down 10.2 percent on a closing volume of nearly 14 million shares.

In London, it hit a low of 88 pence before recovering to end around 94 pence, down 12p, with nearly 2.5 million shares traded. Wednesday's losses followed a fall of more than eight percent to eight francs in Paris on Tuesday.
That compares with an all-time high of 120 francs and a 1987 stock market flotation price of 35 francs.

"The stock's no longer worth anything. It could fall to one franc, two francs, 50 centimes, nothing would shock me," said one Paris-based analyst. But it could equally well rise to 10 francs if short-sellers bought back, he said.

While no one believes the tunnel rail link between Britain and France can fail to make money, the stockmarkets are disappointed by the deal which the company has struck with its banks to try to mitigate the vicious repayment burden of 70 billion francs ($13.53 billion) in debts.

Eurotunnel has agreed that its 225 creditor banks will get 45.5 percent of the company's capital in an equity-for-debt deal which awards the shares to the banks at 10.40 francs each. It could boost their stake later to 54.5 percent -- assuming the deal gets the backing of reluctant small-time shareholders.
For hard-nosed investors, the payback is for the very long term, with the first dividend to shareholders expected at best by the year 2004.
Richard Hannah, a veteran London analyst with a dim view of Eurotunnel's stock prospects, said there was still a question over the solidity of the refinancing long term.
"We think the shares are seriously overvalued at the moment and that's before the dilution (of holdings) comes," he said.

It all makes sad reading for a company which ran up massive debts on an equally massive engineering project without state support. It has been buckling under those debts ever since the tunnel with its high speed train service opened in 1994.
"People are really disappointed with the (restructuring) plan -- no abandoning of loans, 3.5 billion of financial costs a year.
"We've worked it out -- to pay a dividend of one franc you'd need an operating result of 6.5 to seven billion francs a year, and that's not going to come overnight," said one Paris trader.
"The fundamentals are buried by the speculative." ($1=5.172 French Franc)
